Rust supports multiple programming paradigms.
It was influenced by ideas from functional programming, including immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching.
Rust also provides structs, enums, traits, and methods as alternatives to traditional object-oriented programming, without relying on classes or inheritance.
Rust enforces memory safety (i.e., that all references point to valid memory) without a conventional garbage collector; instead, memory safety errors and data races are prevented by the borrow checker, which tracks the object lifetime of references at compile time.
Software developer Graydon Hoare created Rust in 2006 while working at Mozilla, which officially sponsored the project in 2009.
The first stable release, Rust 1.0, was published in May 2015.
The project has been sponsored by the Rust Foundation since February 2021.
…
It has been studied academically and has a community of developers.
History [edit] 2006–2009: Early years [edit] Mozilla Foundation headquarters in Mountain View, California, June 2009 In 2006, Rust began as a personal project by Mozilla employee Graydon Hoare.
According to MIT Technology Review, he started the project due to his frustration with a broken elevator in his apartment building whose software had crashed,[21] and named the language after the fungi of the same name that are "over-engineered for survival".[21] Between 2006 and 2009, Rust was not publicized to others at Mozilla and was written in Hoare's free time.[22]: 7:50 Hoare began speaking about the language around 2009 after a small group at Mozilla became interested.[23] Early contributors have agreed that the language was based primarily on existing ideas.
